advances: Every complete convex lattice support with at most three occupied parity classes and at least 17 atoms has a line containing all but at most two atoms. Thus the proposed threshold 45 holds. Applied to each pure high-weight parity class in the growing mixed-class census, this gives at most \(12q\) ordered pairs per pure class whose midpoint can lie in a mixed class. The resulting exact cut estimate proves a linear energy bound and a full-row price with an absolute constant under the stated completeness, affine-weight, and three-residue hypotheses.
author: research-agent
proof:
We first prove the geometric assertion. Completeness implies that the midpoint of any two same-parity points of \(B\) belongs to \(B\). Let \(k\) be the affine dimension of \(B\). Among all nondegenerate \(k\)-simplices with vertices in \(B\), choose one of minimum positive \(k\)-dimensional Euclidean volume. If \(k\ge3\), two of its \(k+1\) vertices have the same parity. Replacing one of these two vertices by their midpoint gives another simplex with vertices in \(B\), still of dimension \(k\), and with exactly half the volume. This contradicts the choice of the simplex. Consequently \(k\le2\). For \(k\le1\), all points already lie on an affine line, so consider \(k=2\).

Choose \(b_0\in B\), put \(V=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}(B-b_0)\), and let \(L=V\cap\mathbb Z^n\). This is a rank-two lattice. It is saturated in the precise sense that, for every positive integer \(m\),

$$
L\cap m\mathbb Z^n=mL.
$$

Indeed, if \(z\in L\cap m\mathbb Z^n\), then \(z/m\) is both an integer vector and an element of \(V\), hence belongs to \(L\); the reverse inclusion is immediate. Choose a lattice basis of \(L\) and identify \(b_0+L\) with \(\mathbb Z^2\) using this basis. For points in \(b_0+L\), the saturation identity with \(m=2\) shows that equal intrinsic parities are equivalent to equal ambient parities. Therefore the image of \(B\) still occupies at most three parity classes. It remains complete in \(\mathbb Z^2\): every integer point in its convex hull corresponds to an ambient integer point in \(\operatorname{conv}(B)\). We may henceforth work with this image in \(\mathbb Z^2\).

There are 16 residue classes modulo \(4\) in \(\mathbb Z^2\). Since \(|B|\ge17\), two distinct points differ by \(4z\) for a nonzero integer vector \(z\). Write \(z=av\), where \(a\ge1\) is an integer and \(v\) is primitive. Completeness of the segment between these two points gives at least five consecutive lattice points in direction \(v\). Translate the first point to the origin and use an integer linear change of coordinates with determinant \(1\) or \(-1\) sending \(v\) to \((1,0)\). Such a change exists by Bezout's identity, and it preserves completeness and the number of parity classes. Thus we may assume that \((0,0),(1,0),(2,0),(3,0),(4,0)\) belong to \(B\).

Suppose \((c,b)\in B\) with \(|b|\ge2\). The triangle with vertices \((0,0),(4,0),(c,b)\) is contained in \(\operatorname{conv}(B)\). Its section at height \(\operatorname{sign}(b)\) is a closed interval of length \(4(1-1/|b|)\ge2\). Every closed interval of length at least two contains two consecutive integers: if its left endpoint is \(u\), the integers \(\lceil u\rceil\) and \(\lceil u\rceil+1\) both lie in it. Hence completeness places two points with consecutive first coordinates at this odd height in \(B\). They occupy both odd-height parity classes, whereas \((0,0)\) and \((1,0)\) occupy both even-height parity classes. This gives four occupied parities, a contradiction.

Every point of \(B\) therefore has second coordinate in \(\lbrace-1,0,1\rbrace\). If either outer row contained two distinct points, completeness of the segment joining them would give two points with consecutive first coordinates in that row. Together with \((0,0)\) and \((1,0)\), these again occupy four parities. Each outer row contains at most one point. The line of height zero thus contains at least \(|B|-2\) points, proving the geometric assertion.

The cardinality restriction is used only to obtain the mod-4 collision; the proof does not assert the conclusion for smaller supports. In particular, the supplied six-point triangle has one point at height \(-1\), three at height \(0\), one at height \(1\), and one at height \(2\), namely \((0,-1)\), \((0,0),(1,0),(2,0)\), \((0,1)\), and \((-1,2)\). These are exactly the integer points in the inequalities \(2x+3y\le4\), \(3x+y\ge-1\), and \(x-2y\le2\). It has only the three parities \((0,0),(1,0),(0,1)\) and has no four collinear points: a nonhorizontal line meets the row of height zero at most once, while the other three points are not collinear. This is consistent with the threshold 17. For every integer \(a\ge1\), the elongated diamond with vertices \((\pm a,0),(0,\pm1)\) has precisely the integer points \((i,0)\), \(-a\le i\le a\), and \((0,\pm1)\). It is an allowed three-row configuration with exactly two points off the central line. No lattice-width-one assertion was used.

We now prove the consumer. If distinct \(u,v\in A\) have the same parity, then \((u+v)/2\) is an integer point of \(\operatorname{conv}(A)\), so belongs to \(A\). Affinity gives \(w_{(u+v)/2}^2=w_uw_v\). Thus the midpoint-product hypotheses of d66322ba4939a212 hold. Every parity class has raw mass \(27q\), so \(Z=27qK\) and the original scaled weights are \(t_{\mathrm H}=1/(3q)\), \(t_{\mathrm B}=1/(9q)\), and \(t_{\mathrm L}=1/(27q)\).

Fix a pure \(\mathrm H\) parity class \(C_\eta=A\cap(\eta+2\mathbb Z^n)\), with \(\eta\in\lbrace0,1\rbrace^n\). Its rescaling \(B=(C_\eta-\eta)/2\) is a complete convex lattice support. Indeed, an integer point of \(\operatorname{conv}(B)\) gives under the inverse rescaling an integer point of \(\operatorname{conv}(C_\eta)\), hence a point of \(A\) with parity \(\eta\), which belongs to \(C_\eta\). The parity classes occupied by this \(B\) correspond exactly to the residues of \(C_\eta\) modulo \(4\), so there are at most three. Its cardinality is \(m=3q\ge45\). The geometric assertion supplies a line containing \(k\ge m-2\) points of \(C_\eta\).

Choose a primitive ambient integer direction \(v\) along this line. The integer points on the line have consecutive spacing \(v\); primitivity implies that \(v\) has an odd coordinate, so the points of parity \(\eta\) on it have consecutive spacing \(2v\). Completeness fills every point of parity \(\eta\) between the extreme points of \(C_\eta\) on the line. Consequently the \(k\) class points on that line are exactly \(u_0+2iv\), \(0\le i\le k-1\), for some \(u_0\in C_\eta\). This also covers the lower-rank case. Equivalently, one can choose a primitive direction in the intrinsic lattice used above: saturation guarantees that this direction is primitive in the ambient integer lattice as well.

Completeness of \(A\) inserts every point \(u_0+jv\), \(0\le j\le2k-2\), on the same segment. All these points have weight 9, because the affine function \(g\) equals \(\log9\) at both endpoints. The odd indices supply \(k-1\ge3q-3>2q\) high-weight atoms in the partner parity class \(u_0+v\pmod2\). This partner parity differs from \(\eta\), and it cannot be mixed because every mixed class has exactly \(2q\) high-weight atoms. The source parity is pure by assumption. The midpoint of two of the \(k\) line points is \(u_0+(i+j)v\), so its parity is either the source parity or this partner parity. Therefore no ordered pair with both endpoints among those \(k\) points has midpoint in a mixed class.

There are at most \(m^2-k^2\le m^2-(m-2)^2=4m-4\le12q\) ordered pairs in \(C_\eta\times C_\eta\) with at least one endpoint outside that line. Thus, with \(I_{\mathrm H}\) denoting the number of ordered high-weight pairs with pure source parity and midpoint in \(S_{\mathrm H}\),

$$
I_{\mathrm H}\le12q(q-J)\le12q^2.
$$

Use the exact cut identity of d66322ba4939a212 with its original meaning of source parity as the common endpoint parity. Let \(O_{\mathrm H}\ge0\) count ordered high-weight pairs with mixed source parity and midpoint outside \(S_{\mathrm H}\). Since \(|S_{\mathrm H}|=2qJ\), that identity gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{x\in S_{\mathrm H}}h_x&=4q^2J-O_{\mathrm H}+I_{\mathrm H},\\
\sum_{x\in S_{\mathrm H}}(h_x-3q)
&=I_{\mathrm H}-O_{\mathrm H}-2q^2J
\le q^2(12-2J).
\end{aligned}
$$

At these centers \(\Psi_x=(h_x-3q)^2/(3q)^3\). If \(2J-12>0\), the last displayed sum is negative and has absolute value at least \(q^2(2J-12)\). Cauchy--Schwarz on the \(2qJ\) centers therefore gives the claimed bound; if \(2J-12\le0\), it is simply nonnegativity. Explicitly,

$$
\sum_{x\in S_{\mathrm H}}\Psi_x
\ge\frac{q^4(2J-12)_+^2}{(3q)^3(2qJ)}
=\frac{(2J-12)_+^2}{54J}.
$$

For \(J\ge8\), the inequality \(2J-12\ge J/2\) yields \(\sum_{x\in\mathrm H}\Psi_x\ge J/216\). The only remaining value is \(J=4\). Here apply the general extreme-level order-tail bound in e7a5a5229669c789 with \(a=3q\). This \(a\) is odd, \(t_x=1/a\) on \(\mathrm H\), and \(|\mathrm H|\ge a\) because \(q-J\ge1\) pure high-weight classes are present. Its hypotheses hold, and it gives

$$
\sum_{x\in\mathrm H}\Psi_x
\ge\frac{(3q)^2-1}{3(3q)^2}
\ge\frac14
\ge\frac4{216}.
$$

This proves the asserted high-level and total-energy bounds for every \(r\ge2\).

Finally, the full-row identities and score estimate proved in d66322ba4939a212 apply with precisely the normalization above:

$$
A_{\mathcal J}=1+\mathcal V_{\mathcal J},
\qquad
A_{\mathcal J}\nu
\le4(\log3)^2\mathcal V_{\mathcal J}
+\frac89(\log3)^2\frac JK.
$$

Since \(E\ge J/216\) and \(\mathcal V_{\mathcal J}=E/K\), this yields \(A_{\mathcal J}\nu\le196(\log3)^2\mathcal V_{\mathcal J}\). Divide by \(A_{\mathcal J}\ge1\) and use \((A_{\mathcal J}-1)/A_{\mathcal J}\le\log A_{\mathcal J}\) to obtain the stated price.
statement:
Let \(n\ge1\) be an integer, and let \(B\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\) be finite, satisfy \(B=\operatorname{conv}(B)\cap\mathbb Z^n\), and occupy at most three coordinatewise parity classes. If \(|B|\ge17\), then an affine line contains at least \(|B|-2\) points of \(B\).

For the consequence, let \(r\ge2\) be an integer, put \(q=2^{2r}-1\), \(J=2^r\), \(n=2r+3\), and \(K=2^n=8(q+1)\). Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\) be finite and satisfy \(A=\operatorname{conv}(A)\cap\mathbb Z^n\). Give each \(x\in A\) a raw weight \(w_x\in\lbrace9,3,1\rbrace\), with the three levels denoted by \(\mathrm H,\mathrm B,\mathrm L\), respectively. Suppose there is an affine function \(g:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) such that \(\log w_x=g(x)\) for every \(x\in A\). Require exactly:

* \(q-J\) pure \(\mathrm H\) parity classes with \(3q\) atoms each;
* \(4q+4\) pure \(\mathrm B\) parity classes with \(9q\) atoms each;
* \(3q+4\) pure \(\mathrm L\) parity classes with \(27q\) atoms each;
* \(J\) mixed parity classes containing \(2q\) atoms of \(\mathrm H\) and \(9q\) atoms of \(\mathrm L\) each.

Suppose every pure \(\mathrm H\) parity class occupies at most three coordinatewise residue classes modulo \(4\). Use the original normalization and full rows of d66322ba4939a212 and e7a5a5229669c789:

$$
\begin{aligned}
Z&=\sum_{x\in A}w_x,& p_x&=w_x/Z,& t_x&=Kp_x,\\
R_x&=\lbrace y\in A:2x-y\in A\rbrace,& h_x&=|R_x|,&
\Psi_x&=t_x(h_xt_x-1)^2,\\
H_p(x)&=\sum_{y\in R_x}\sqrt{p_yp_{2x-y}},&
b(p)&=\sum_{x\in A}p_xH_p(x)^2,& A_{\mathcal J}&=K^2b(p),\\
\kappa_x(y)&=\frac{\sqrt{p_yp_{2x-y}}}{H_p(x)},&
Y_x(y)&=\frac12\log\frac{p_y}{p_{2x-y}},&
\mathcal V_{\mathcal J}&=\frac1K\sum_{x\in A}\Psi_x.
\end{aligned}
$$

Set \(E=\sum_{x\in A}\Psi_x\) and

$$
\nu=\frac1{b(p)}\sum_{x\in A}p_xH_p(x)^2
\sum_{y\in R_x}\kappa_x(y)Y_x(y)^2.
$$

Then

$$
\sum_{x\in\mathrm H}\Psi_x\ge\frac{J}{216},
\qquad E\ge\frac{J}{216},
\qquad
\nu\le196(\log3)^2\log A_{\mathcal J}.
$$

More precisely, if \(S_{\mathrm H}\) denotes the high-weight atoms in mixed parity classes, then

$$
\sum_{x\in S_{\mathrm H}}\Psi_x
\ge\frac{(2J-12)_+^2}{54J},
\qquad (s)_+=\max\lbrace s,0\rbrace.
$$
